1051.title: Nicholas (6 December)
1051.hook: a bishop who secretly gave dowries to three poor girls, the root of Santa Claus
1051.howItsDone: Saint Nicholas is remembered on 6 December; in parts of Europe children set out shoes or stockings the night before and find small gifts in the morning, and some parishes collect gifts for the poor around his feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andrew, who spent an afternoon with Jesus and went home to get his brother. Your line was he brought his brother. Did you connect two people? Day one thousand fifty-one.

A bag of gold sails through an open window in the dark and lands on the floor of a poor man's house. Nobody sees who threw it. The man has three daughters and no money for their dowries, and in that world, the story says, it meant they had no good future ahead of them. Now one of them can marry. A while later, another bag comes through the window. Then the father decides he has to know. He waits up. Today, the man he catches at the window: Nicholas.
screen: `GOLD THROUGH A DARK WINDOW.` → `THREE DAUGHTERS, NO DOWRY.` → `THE FATHER WAITS UP.`

segments.voice: Nicholas was a bishop of Myra, a town on the southern coast of what is now Turkey. Very little is known for certain about his life. What came down instead is a set of stories, and the dowry story is the one that stuck. In the telling, Nicholas has inherited money and wants to help the family without being seen. So he goes at night, three times. On the third night the father runs out and catches him, and falls at his feet. And Nicholas asks him for one thing: tell no one. That request is the heart of it. Jesus says it in the Sermon on the Mount. In the Douay-Rheims: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." And the promise that follows: "thy Father who seeth in secret will repay thee." Nicholas wanted the gift to be all gift, with no thank-you note coming back to him. There's a small irony here. The father clearly didn't keep the secret, or we'd never have heard it. And the secret giver ended up with a very public afterlife. In the Netherlands he became Sinterklaas, and the usual account traces Santa Claus to that Dutch name. In parts of Europe, children still set out shoes on the eve of his feast and find small gifts in them by morning. Under the red suit and the reindeer is a bishop at a window, throwing gold into the dark and hoping not to be seen.
screen: `A BISHOP OF MYRA.` · `THREE NIGHTS, AND THEN: TELL NO ONE.` · `LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.` · `FROM SINTERKLAAS TO SANTA CLAUS.` · then, large: `THY FATHER WHO SEETH IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a secret gift. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Think of someone who could use a lift right now. Not a grand gesture. Coffee paid for, a note left on a desk, a bill quietly covered, a chore done before anyone wakes up. Choose one, and work out how to do it so they never find out it was you. Notice how it feels to give up the thank-you in advance. If you pray, you can offer the gift to God before you give it. The bell holds the time.
Nicholas. The bishop of Myra who threw dowries through a poor man's window at night, asked to stay unknown, and became the root of Santa Claus.
Your line: in secret. Today, do the gift you planned, and then keep it to yourself. Don't tell anyone, not even later as a good story. Day one thousand fifty-one.

1052.title: Juan Diego (9 December)
1052.howItsDone: Saint Juan Diego is remembered on 9 December, shortly before the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe; pilgrims visit the basilica at Tepeyac, where the tilma is kept, especially in those days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicholas, the bishop at the window with a bag of gold. Your line was in secret. Did your gift stay secret? Day one thousand fifty-two.

Birdsong, before sunrise, on a bare hill called Tepeyac, which today lies inside Mexico City. An Indigenous man named Juan Diego is walking past on his way to church when the singing stops him. Then a woman's voice calls him by name, gently, the way you'd call a child. He climbs toward it and finds a Lady standing on the hill, shining. She has an errand for him: go to the bishop and ask that a church be built right here. Today, the messenger she picked.
screen: `BIRDSONG ON TEPEYAC.` → `A VOICE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `GO TO THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Nican Mopohua, an account written in Nahuatl, Juan Diego's own language. And the way the Lady talks to him is the first surprise. She uses tender forms: my littlest one, my youngest child. The Nahuatl word is noxocoyouh. Juan Diego goes to the bishop, waits, and is politely doubted. He comes back and does something very human: he asks her to send someone else. In the account he calls himself a nobody, small, not the kind of man bishops listen to. Please, send someone important. She refuses. She has plenty of messengers, she says, but it's him she wants. Then his uncle falls gravely ill, and Juan Diego, running for a priest, takes a different path around the hill so he won't have to face her and explain. She comes down and meets him anyway. She tells him his uncle is already well, and asks, in effect, whether he has forgotten that she is his mother and he is under her care. Then she sends him up the hill to gather flowers, in a season when nothing should be blooming. He carries them to the bishop folded in his tilma, his cloak. He opens it, the flowers fall, and on the cloth is the image of the Lady that pilgrims still visit at Guadalupe. Mary's own song in Luke says it plainly. In the Douay-Rheims: "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble." The bishop needed a sign. The sign came in the hands of the man who thought he didn't count.
screen: `MY LITTLEST ONE: NOXOCOYOUH.` · `PLEASE, SEND SOMEONE IMPORTANT.` · `HE TAKES THE OTHER PATH; SHE FINDS HIM.` · `FLOWERS, A CLOAK, AN IMAGE.` · then, large: `AND HATH EXALTED THE HUMBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a humble messenger. Settle and breathe. Think of the people who bring things to you and are rarely noticed. The mail carrier. The delivery driver. The person who cleans the building after everyone leaves. The one who answers the phone. Choose one face. Hold it in mind and remember one thing they've carried to you. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name, or by their job if you don't know the name. If you don't, plan how you'll thank them in person. The bell holds the time.
Juan Diego. The Indigenous man of Tepeyac who asked to be replaced by someone important, and was chosen anyway, his cloak full of flowers.
Your line: the littlest son. Today, thank one person who carries things for a living, by name if you can, and look them in the eye. Day one thousand fifty-two.

1053.title: Our Lady of Loreto (10 December)
1053.hook: a shrine honoring the house of Nazareth, patron of pilots
1053.howItsDone: Our Lady of Loreto is remembered on 10 December; pilgrims visit the Holy House inside the basilica at Loreto, and some air travelers and crews ask her protection before flights.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Juan Diego, who asked to be replaced and was chosen anyway. Your line was the littlest son. Did you thank someone who carries things for a living? Day one thousand fifty-three.

Rough stone walls. A small, plain room, the kind of room a family once lived in. And around it, a great church on a hilltop in Loreto, in central Italy, built to hold this one plain room like a jewel box holds a ring. Pilgrims shuffle in, touch the walls, and some kneel on the floor. Why would anyone build a basilica around a room this ordinary? Because of whose room, tradition says, it was.
screen: `A SMALL ROOM OF ROUGH STONE.` → `A GREAT CHURCH AROUND IT.` → `WHOSE ROOM WAS IT?`

segments.voice: Tradition holds that this is the house of Nazareth, the house of Mary, where the angel came to her. Luke's gospel sets the scene. In the Douay-Rheims: "the angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee, called Nazareth." Notice where God's message lands: not in a temple, but in a small town, in someone's home. Then comes the legend. The story says that when the house was in danger, angels lifted it and carried it through the air, setting it down at last on the hill at Loreto. Some historians suggest a plainer route: people, not angels, moving the stones and rebuilding them. The feast doesn't depend on settling that. What it honors is the house, and what happened in it. John's gospel says it in one line: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Dwelt. Lived somewhere. Had a door, a table, a floor that needed sweeping. For Catholics who pray at Loreto, the shrine is a way of touching that ordinary home where, they believe, the Son of God grew up. And the flying house had a modern sequel. Because of the legend, Our Lady of Loreto became the patron of pilots and air travelers, and some people still say a prayer to her before a flight. A litany of titles for Mary is named for this shrine, too: the Litany of Loreto, prayed there and far beyond. A plain room, honored because, in the story, God came to an ordinary house.
screen: `THE HOUSE OF NAZARETH, TRADITION SAYS.` · `CARRIED BY ANGELS, THE LEGEND SAYS.` · `THE WORD DWELT AMONG US.` · `PATRON OF PILOTS AND TRAVELERS.` · then, large: `AND THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for travelers by air. Settle and breathe. Right now, somewhere above you, planes are in the air: pilots watching their instruments, crews pouring coffee, passengers asleep against the window, someone flying home to a hospital bed, someone flying toward a new job. If you know someone traveling, hold them first. Then widen it to everyone up there. If you pray, you can ask Our Lady of Loreto to watch over them. If you don't, simply wish them a safe landing, one face at a time. The bell holds the time.
Our Lady of Loreto. Mary honored at the shrine of the holy house, which tradition holds to be her home in Nazareth, and patron of those who fly.
Your line: the holy house. Today, do one ordinary chore at home slowly and carefully, as if the room you're cleaning mattered. Day one thousand fifty-three.

1054.title: Lucy (13 December)
1054.hook: a Sicilian martyr whose name sounds like light, honored with candles in dark Scandinavia
1054.howItsDone: Saint Lucy is remembered on 13 December; in Sweden and other Nordic countries the day is kept with processions of singers in white led by a girl wearing a crown of candles, and in Sicily with special foods and Masses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of Loreto and the small stone room. Your line was the holy house. Did you do one ordinary chore slowly? Day one thousand fifty-four.

It's still pitch dark outside on a December morning in Sweden. A door opens and a girl in a long white dress walks in, slowly, because she's wearing a crown of lit candles on her head. Behind her comes a line of others in white, each holding one candle, singing. Families, schools and churches in Sweden and its neighbors keep some version of this morning. The girl is dressed as a saint. Not a Viking, not a winter spirit. A young martyr from Sicily, a long way south. Today, Lucy.
screen: `A DARK SWEDISH MORNING.` → `A CROWN OF CANDLES.` → `A SAINT FROM SICILY.`

segments.voice: Lucy was a martyr of Syracuse, in Sicily. Like Cecilia last week, she is one of the women martyrs named in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Roman Missal. Beyond her name, her story comes from her legend. In the story, she decides to give her life to God, and she gives her dowry away to the poor. The young man she was expected to marry is furious and reports her as a Christian. The authorities try to drag her off to shame her, and in the legend they cannot move her at all. Not with ropes, not with a team of oxen. She stands there like a pillar. She dies by the sword. Now, the light. Lucy's name sounds like lux, the Latin for light, and the people who told her story leaned into it. Paintings show her holding a lamp, or carrying her eyes on a dish, and she became the patron of people with trouble seeing. Her feast falls in the dark weeks of the northern winter, and some say that is part of why the north took her to heart. John's gospel puts it in one line. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." The Lucy morning acts that verse out. Somebody walks into the dark room carrying light, and the room doesn't get to stay dark. A martyr who gave her dowry away became, far from home, the girl who brings the morning in.
screen: `A MARTYR OF SYRACUSE.` · `HER DOWRY GIVEN TO THE POOR.` · `THEY CANNOT MOVE HER.` · `A NAME THAT SOUNDS LIKE LIGHT.` · then, large: `AND THE LIGHT SHINETH IN DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring a little light in. If you have a candle and it's safe, light it now. If not, sit in a dim spot and switch on one small lamp. Watch the flame or the glow. Notice how far one small light reaches, and where it stops. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can hold the people in your life who are in a dark stretch right now, one at a time, in that light. If you don't, simply stay with the glow. Tomorrow, try lighting it first thing in the morning. The bell holds the time.
Lucy. The martyr of Syracuse who gave her dowry to the poor, whose feast brings candles into the dark weeks of December.
Your line: light in december. Today, be the one who walks into a gloomy room, or a gloomy conversation, and brings something bright with you. Day one thousand fifty-four.

1055.title: John of Kanty (23 December)
1055.hook: a Kraków professor who gave away his coat and shoes
1055.howItsDone: Saint John of Kanty is remembered on 23 December, especially in Poland and at the university in Kraków where he taught; some parishes and schools collect coats and warm clothing around his feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lucy, the martyr of Syracuse and the crown of candles. Your line was light in december. Did you bring a little light into a room? Day one thousand fifty-five.

A professor walks home through a winter street in Kraków, wearing the long gown of a university teacher. It sweeps the ground as he goes. If you lifted the hem, the story says, you would find his feet bare in the cold. Earlier, on the way, he met a poor man with nothing on his feet, and handed over his own shoes. The gown is long enough that nobody notices. A man who lectured on God all day, walking home on cold stone. Today, John of Kanty.
screen: `A PROFESSOR IN A LONG GOWN.` → `BARE FEET UNDER THE HEM.` → `A LECTURER ON COLD STONE.`

segments.voice: John of Kanty was a priest who taught at the university in Kraków. His job was ideas: lectures, books, students, arguments about God. But the stories people kept about him are about clothes, food and money leaving his hands. Tradition says he gave his coat to a man shivering in the street, and on another day his shoes. When a hungry person came to the door during a meal, he was known to send his own plate out. There's a story about robbers, too. Thieves stopped him on the road, took what he had, and asked if there was anything more. He said no. Then he found a few coins sewn into his clothes, and he ran after the robbers to hand them over, because he had told them there was nothing left. They were so shaken, the story goes, that they gave everything back. Behind all this is a very plain line from Luke's gospel. The crowds ask John the Baptist what they should do, and he answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none." No theory. Just coats. Jesus, in the parable of the last judgment, lists what the blessed did for him without knowing it, and one line is: "Naked, and you covered me." A professor could have lectured on those verses. The stories remember him doing them, in the snow, with cold feet under his gown. His feast falls on 23 December, two days before Christmas, when the coats come out of the closet.
screen: `A PROFESSOR WHOSE JOB WAS IDEAS.` · `HIS COAT, HIS SHOES, HIS PLATE.` · `HE RAN AFTER THE ROBBERS.` · `TWO COATS: GIVE ONE AWAY.` · then, large: `NAKED, AND YOU COVERED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a coat to give. Settle and breathe. Picture your closet, or the hooks by your door. Walk through them slowly in your mind. Is there a coat, a sweater, a pair of boots, a warm hat you haven't worn in a long time? Choose one. Picture who might be cold without it this winter. Then think of where you could take it: a shelter, a coat drive, a parish collection, a neighbor. If you pray, you can offer it to God before it goes. The bell holds the time.
John of Kanty. The Kraków professor whose learning was real, but who is remembered for the coat and shoes he gave away, even in the snow.
Your line: the professor's coat. Today, take that coat out of the closet and put it in a bag by the door, so it actually leaves the house. Day one thousand fifty-five.

1056.title: Adam and Eve (24 December)
1056.hook: some old calendars honor our first parents on Christmas Eve
1056.howItsDone: Adam and Eve are not on today's General Roman Calendar, but some older Western calendars and devotions remembered them on 24 December, and Catholics hear the garden story at Mass on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, where it is set beside Mary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of Kanty, the professor with bare feet under his gown. Your line was the professor's coat. Did a coat make it into a bag by the door? Day one thousand fifty-six.

On the day before Christmas, some old calendars of saints didn't name a martyr or a bishop. They named two people from the very first pages of the Bible: Adam and Eve. Tradition says that in parts of medieval Europe, people acted out the story of the garden around this day, with a tree hung with fruit standing in the middle of the stage. Some historians connect that tree, at least in part, with the Christmas tree. So why would anyone put the garden right next to the manger?
screen: `CHRISTMAS EVE IN OLD CALENDARS.` → `A TREE HUNG WITH FRUIT.` → `THE GARDEN NEXT TO THE MANGER.`

segments.voice: Start with how Genesis tells it. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Mud and breath. That's the human being in this story: made of the ground, alive with God's own breath. Then the woman, made from Adam's side, and a garden with one tree whose fruit they are told not to eat. The rest is the famous part. Notice that the text never says apple; it says the fruit of the tree. The apple came later, in art and plays. They eat, they hide, they are sent out of the garden. And before they leave, Adam names his wife. "And Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all the living." Even on the edge of leaving paradise, the story puts a name of life on her. That's why the day before Christmas fits. Catholic tradition reads the Bible as one story, and Christmas as a turning point in it. Paul puts the two ends side by side: "And as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive." He even calls Christ the last Adam. Early Christian writers added a second pair, calling Mary the new Eve, the woman whose yes undoes the first no. So on Christmas Eve, the old calendars remembered the first parents, waiting, as it were, at the door of the stable. And there's one more thing in Eve's name. If she is the mother of all the living, then every person you will meet today is, in this story, a cousin.
screen: `MUD AND BREATH: A LIVING SOUL.` · `THE FRUIT, NOT AN APPLE.` · `EVE: MOTHER OF ALL THE LIVING.` · `IN ADAM ALL DIE; IN CHRIST, ALIVE.` · then, large: `THE MOTHER OF ALL THE LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the whole human family. Settle, and notice your breath, the breath of life in the story. Begin with one face, someone close to you. Then widen: the people on your street. Your town. The people you argue with. Strangers on the other side of the world, waking up as you go to sleep. Let the circle keep growing until it holds everyone. If you pray, you can say the first two words of the Lord's Prayer, Our Father, and notice the word our. If you don't, simply let the word family stretch as far as it will go. The bell holds the time.
Adam and Eve. In Genesis, the first parents, made of earth and breath, remembered in some old calendars on Christmas Eve, the night the story turns.

Your line: the first parents. Today, when someone gets on your nerves, remember that in this story they are family, and treat them like a cousin you'll see again at the holidays. Day one thousand fifty-six.

1057.title: John the Evangelist (27 December)
1057.hook: the beloved disciple, the eagle, and the one the fourth Gospel places at the cross
1057.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint John, apostle and evangelist, on 27 December, inside the Christmas octave; in some places wine is blessed on his day, a custom tied to a story people tell about him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adam and Eve, kept on Christmas Eve in some old calendars. Your line was the first parents. Did you pray, or simply hope, for the whole human family? Day one thousand fifty-seven.

"Lord, who is it?" A question asked at supper on the night before the cross. Jesus has just said that one of the twelve will betray him. Peter wants a name, so he signals to the disciple closest to Jesus, the one leaning against his chest. That disciple leans back and asks the question. The Gospel never gives him a name in that scene. It gives him a description instead. Today, two days after Christmas, the Church keeps the feast of the man tradition says that description belongs to.
screen: `LORD, WHO IS IT?` → `PETER SIGNALS.` → `A HEAD RESTING AGAINST JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the description, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." The Gospel of John comes back to that description more than once, the disciple whom Jesus loved, and never calls him by name. The Church's tradition identifies him with John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, and names the fourth Gospel after him. Some modern readers wonder whether the beloved disciple was someone else. The text itself leaves him unnamed, and that silence may be the point: a disciple described only by being loved. Then the cross. The fourth Gospel places him there, standing beside the mother of Jesus. Jesus looks at the two of them and says to her, "Woman, behold thy son." And to him, "Behold thy mother." From that hour, the Gospel says, the disciple took her into his own home. Catholic tradition reads that moment as Mary being given to every disciple, not only to one. On Easter morning he runs to the empty tomb with Peter and gets there first. And at the very end, the Gospel says this disciple is the one who bears witness to these things and wrote them down. In Christian art he is often painted with an eagle. Tradition gives each Gospel writer a living creature from the visions of Ezekiel and the Apocalypse, and John gets the eagle; the traditional explanation is that his Gospel flies high from its opening line, In the beginning was the Word. So one man carries both pictures: the eagle soaring, and the head resting quietly on a friend's chest. This week we walked with Nicholas giving in secret, Juan Diego the littlest son, the holy house of Loreto, Lucy's light, John of Kanty's coat, and our first parents. Today the week ends at the supper table.
